q: What is the difference between the EU ETS and CBAM, and how are they linked?
title: EU ETS vs CBAM: the difference
short: The EU ETS puts a carbon price on emissions from plants inside the EU. CBAM puts the same price on the embedded emissions of certain imported goods. They are linked in two ways: the CBAM certificate price follows EU ETS auction prices, and CBAM charges grow as free ETS allowances for EU producers are phased out.

ul: Who pays: ETS, operators of EU installations such as steel works, cement kilns and power plants. CBAM, the authorised CBAM declarant who imports covered goods into the EU.
What is priced: ETS, the installation's own verified emissions each year. CBAM, the embedded emissions in imported cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity.
The unit: ETS, allowances (one tonne CO2e each). CBAM, CBAM certificates (one tonne CO2e each).
Trading: ETS allowances are auctioned and traded freely. CBAM certificates are bought through the central platform and cannot be traded between declarants.

p: The CBAM certificate price is set from EU ETS allowance auction prices. For certificates covering 2026 imports the price is a quarterly average of auction prices; from 2027 it is a weekly average. An Indian exporter's CBAM exposure therefore moves with the EU carbon market even though the exporter is not in the ETS.

EU producers in CBAM sectors still receive some free ETS allowances. To avoid charging importers more than domestic producers, the number of CBAM certificates owed is reduced by an amount that reflects that free allocation. As free allocation is phased down from 2026 to 2034, that reduction shrinks and the CBAM charge on the same tonne rises, reaching the full price in 2034.

sections.h: What this means for an Indian exporter
ul: You do not buy ETS allowances or CBAM certificates; your EU buyer does, and the cost shows up in price negotiations.
Actual, verified embedded emissions usually cost the buyer less than default values, which carry mark-ups.
A carbon price effectively paid in India can be deducted under CBAM Article 9, but only with evidence; check whether any Indian charge qualifies before relying on it.
